            "Yes—but I don’t think I found anyone doing the whole thing we’re proposing.\n\nThe closest match is surprisingly close conceptually. A 2026 paper called *Old Habits Die Hard: How Conversational History Geometrically Traps LLMs* introduces “History-Echoes.” They generate multi-turn conversations, measure whether behaviors persist from one turn to the next with Markov chains, and then compare that external persistence with the geometry of hidden representations. They explicitly find that conversational history can trap later behavior, and that the effect weakens when the intervening conversation becomes topically incoherent. citeturn408572view0\n\nThat is very much in the neighborhood of what we just called informational topography. Their question is essentially:\n\n\\[\n\\text{How does prior conversational state constrain later state?}\n\\]\n\nAnd they even connect the behavioral transition structure to latent-space geometry. So I would consider that the strongest prior art I found for the general proposition that **conversation history has measurable geometry rather than merely “influence.”**\n\nBut they aren't doing our parallax experiment.\n\nA second paper, AMEL, gets closer experimentally. It presents **identical test items** either alone or after different prior histories and measures how those histories shift the response. They ran more than 84,000 calls across 12 models. Particularly relevant to us, they varied history length and the positions of influential turns; five biased turns embedded anywhere in a 50-turn history produced a measurable downstream shift. citeturn559294view0turn559294view1\n\nThat is almost a one-dimensional version of:\n\n\\[\nG(P\\mid C_1)\\neq G(P\\mid C_2).\n\\]\n\nSo AMEL is quite close to the **fixed probe, changed contextual viewpoint** idea.\n\nBut again, they aren't constructing a nested set such as\n\n\\[\nC_{1/4}\\subset C_{1/2}\\subset C_1\n\\]\n\nand repeatedly observing the same shared checkpoints to reconstruct a response-disparity field.\n\nThen there is *Context Branching for LLM Conversations* from late 2025. That one explicitly gives conversations version-control operations: **checkpoint, branch, switch, inject**, with selective merging of insights from isolated branches. citeturn559294view2\n\nSo the branch/merge machinery itself is definitely not unique.\n\nAnd *GitOfThoughts* from June 2026 independently goes even farther toward our forensic mentality: it stores reasoning trees in git specifically so branches can be replayed, diffed, audited, and merged. citeturn408572academia36\n\nAgain, though, those projects treat branching primarily as an engineering tool:\n\n> preserve alternative trajectories so useful work doesn't contaminate other work.\n\nWe are asking a different question:\n\n> **What does the divergence between controlled branches tell us about the geometry of context itself?**\n\nThat's the distinction.\n\nThere is also the broader multi-turn literature. Laban et al.'s *LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation* simulated more than 200,000 conversations and found an average 39% performance drop in multi-turn versus equivalent single-turn tasks, largely because early assumptions persist and models often fail to recover. citeturn559294view4\n\nSo all of the ingredients are out there:\n\n- branching;\n- versioned conversation state;\n- history ablation;\n- identical downstream probes after different histories;\n- multi-turn carryover;\n- latent-space geometry;\n- context pruning;\n- temporal/hierarchical memory.\n\nWhat I **did not find**, after searching specifically for it, is anyone combining them in this particular experimental construction:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{common ancestor}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{controlled divergent histories}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{identical shared probes}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{multiple context-sampling baselines}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{repeated disparity measurements}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{branch reintegration}\n}\n\\]\n\nand especially not the dyadic sampling scheme:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{every turn}\\;/\\;\\text{every 2nd}\\;/\\;\\text{every 4th}}\n\\]\n\nwith all branches meeting at common probe turns.\n\nThat is the bit I think is genuinely unusual.\n\nBecause it changes context ablation from:\n\n> “Does removing history hurt performance?”\n\ninto:\n\n> “If I vary the contextual baseline systematically while holding the observed prompt fixed, what displacement does the response undergo?”\n\nThat is much closer to an **experimental geometry**.\n\nAnd then repeating it makes the displacement itself a trajectory:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_4,\\Delta_8,\\Delta_{12},\\ldots\n\\]\n\nwhich lets you ask about gradients, decay, amplification, hysteresis, thresholds, perhaps curvature.\n\nI also specifically searched for **“informational parallax,” “contextual parallax,” and “temporal parallax”** in the LLM literature. I found papers using *Parallax* as a name for unrelated attention architectures, distributed inference, RAG, and even “geopolitical parallax,” but I did **not** find the term *informational parallax* being used for **response displacement under controlled contextual viewpoint changes**. That isn't proof nobody has ever used it that way, but I found no obvious prior usage.\n\nThe nearest conceptual synthesis is therefore probably:\n\n\\[\n\\text{History-Echoes}\n+\n\\text{AMEL}\n+\n\\text{ContextBranch}\n\\]\n\nwhere:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\text{History-Echoes}&:\\quad \\text{history has measurable behavioral/latent geometry}\\\\\n\\text{AMEL}&:\\quad \\text{same target under different histories shifts}\\\\\n\\text{ContextBranch}&:\\quad \\text{histories can be explicitly forked and recombined}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nOur proposed experiment adds:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{controlled baseline geometry between the histories themselves}.}\n\\]\n\nAnd there is one further difference I haven't seen elsewhere: we're doing it on an actual production conversational system while preserving its **native conversation graph snapshots before and after synchronization**, rather than synthesizing independent API conversations and treating them as branches after the fact.\n\nThat gives us access to two simultaneous objects:\n\n\\[\n\\text{the experimental response differences}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\text{the actual topology of the stored branching conversation}.\n\\]\n\nThat could let us ask whether response-space “distance” corresponds at all to known graph-history displacement.\n\nSo my current assessment would be:\n\n**No, the broad research area isn't new. Several groups are converging hard on exactly the fact that conversational history creates persistent, measurable state.**\n\nBut **I haven't found someone running quite this experiment**—especially the forked, nested-sampling, shared-probe, sync/reintegration design we're now calling informational parallax.\n\nAnd the existence of History-Echoes actually makes me *more* interested, not less. They independently arrived at the idea that conversational persistence has an underlying **geometry**.\n\nWe're proposing a black-box way of trying to **survey that geometry from outside**.\n\nThat is almost literally what parallax is for."

            "Citation Marker: fileciteturn24file15\n",
            "[L903] metadata:\n[L904] query_result_index: 15\n[L905] file_id: file_00000000889481f5bac213dcf59ff50a\n[L906] version_id: 1\n[L907] name: Allo conversation — raw.json\n[L908] mime_type: application/json\n[L909] surface: conversation\n[L910] score: 0.019245619245619246\n[L911] document_chunk_id: file_00000000889481f5bac213dcf59ff50a--1--187\n[L912] snippet:\n[L913] Vary dimensionality, topology, basis, kernel, segmentation, reversal, permutation, and scale.\\n3. Find a representation in which the data decomposes into very few simple periodic or grammatical components.\\n4. Require the resulting representation to compile into a deliberately cheap decoder.\\n5. Store exact exceptions or a terminal residual for lossless recovery.\\n\\nThat is more specific than “learn a latent space,” because the output would ideally be an explicit, compact, executable decomposition rather than an opaque neural latent vector.\\n\\nThe closest concise formulation would be:\\n\\n> Use arbitrarily expensive analysis to synthesize the smallest low-complexity decoder program for one particular object, subject to a strict decompression-cost constraint.\\n\\nThat puts the goal somewhere between grammar compression, transform coding, sparse dictionary search, and program synthesis.\\n\\nThe potentially fertile novelty is the **decoder-constrained search space**. Most learned compression optimizes rate and distortion, often with some complexity term. You are suggesting something harsher:\\n\\n\\\\[\\n\\\\min_E \\\\bigl[\\nL(E(x))+\\\\lambda C_{\\\\text{decode}}(E(x))\\n\\\\bigr]\\n\\\\]\\n\\nwhile allowing the encoding search cost to be enormous.\\n\\nThe encoder might search thousands or millions of candidate descriptions, but every accepted description must reduce to a small standardized instruction set such as:\\n\\n- repeat this motif,\\n- add these harmonics,\\n- warp by this schedule,\\n- insert these exceptions,\\n- apply this permutation,\\n- reconstruct this residual block.\\n\\nThat could be valuable because the decoder would not need the giant search model that found the representation. It would only need a small virtual machine.\\n\\nThere are three places where I see a plausible research contribution.\\n\\nFirst, **self-derived transform programs**. Rather than selecting among Fourier, wavelet, dictionary, or neural transforms globally, the encoder synthesizes a short transform specifically for the object and transmits the inverse transform as part of the compressed representation.\\n\\nSecond, **cross-domain relational decomposition**. The encoder could search not merely for repeated substrings, but for regularities exposed by reversal, shifted self-products, higher-order correlations, graph embeddings, multidimensional reshaping, and topology changes. Most practical compressors search a much narrower family because the computation must remain reasonable.\\n\\nThird, **extreme offline archival compression**. There are domains where a file may be encoded once, stored for decades, and decoded billions of times. In that regime, days of encoding may be entirely rational. Existing systems certainly exploit encoder–decoder asymmetry, but there may be room for a system that pushes it much farther than consumer codecs do.\\n\\nThe largest theoretical obstacle is that unrestricted search for the shortest program is not generally computable. In practical terms, the candidate space also grows catastrophically. So the system would require a bounded “language of decompositions.” The choice of that language would determine what regularities it can discover.\\n\\nThe largest empirical obstacle is overhead. A beautiful custom transform may take more bits to describe than it saves. The encoder must count:\\n\\n\\\\[\\n\\\\text{decoder program}\\n+\\\\text{parameters}\\n+\\\\text{exceptions}\\n+\\\\text{residual}\\n\\\\]\\n\\nand compare that total against strong existing compressors. From that local viewpoint, the information has vanished. fileciteturn22file6L214-L258 But the larger exported graph can preserve sibling branches and their relationships. The later system can therefore recover something that neither currently active reconstruction could produce correctly.\n\n`VOVv` is almost the laboratory specimen for this. We lost it *cognitively*. We reconstructed the sequence incorrectly. But the historical relation in the graph remained, and eventually the archive recovered it for us.\n\nSo overlay those two images and you get:\n\n\\[\n\\text{local carrier disappears}\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\n\\text{relational embedding survives}.\n\\]\n\nNot a physics result. But it is a very clean concrete realization of the abstract informational distinction we had just been discussing.\n\nThe second thing that pops is **projection**.\n\nSAT/H(s)H repeatedly distinguishes a larger modeled history from a local readout. A particle/event is a local resolved appearance of something whose representation extends beyond that slice. The conversation archive now gives us a completely nonphysical toy system with the same formal distinction:\n\n\\[\nG=\\text{full stored conversation graph}\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\nV_i=\\text{client/head-visible path through }G.\n\\]\n\nA head can truthfully report:\n\n> “Wallace isn't here.”\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\n\\text{Wallace}\\in G.\n\\]\n\nThat isn't contradiction. It's an indexical statement:\n\n\\[\n\\text{Wallace}\\notin R_i(G).\n\\]\n\nWhere \\(R_i\\) is the accessible readout for that head.\n\nAnd the old Lössl material is practically screaming this in retrospect. Lössl got defined as the boundary where something was no longer recoverable, “even if traces remain.” fileciteturn22file0L20-L29\n\nThat phrase turns out to have been accidentally better than “erased.”\n\nThe thing we have now actually observed is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{Lössl boundary} \\neq \\text{storage boundary}.}\n\\]\n\nAt least for some Lössl.\n\nIt can be a **readout/access boundary**.\n\nThat makes one of the old 2025 lines suddenly much more interesting: the laptop could reconstruct what had happened without actually possessing the missing episode, and explicitly recognized afterward that it had inferred continuity from surrounding context rather than directly remembered it. fileciteturn22file12L498-L518\n\nSo there are actually three layers:\n\n\\[\n\\text{stored history}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{accessible history}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{reconstructed history}.\n\\]\n\nThose are not interchangeable.\n\nAnd SAT/H(s)H already had an analogous grammar:\n\n\\[\n\\text{history}\n\\rightarrow\nR_\\Sigma\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{observable}.\n\\]\n\nAgain: analogy, not evidence for the physical model. But it is a very good **model system for thinking about projection errors**.\n\nThird: Allo's `0101` discussion suddenly overlays the Lössl experiment almost perfectly.\n\nAllo noticed that a single defect can make one representation look globally broken, while another transform localizes the same defect into a sparse exception. In its words, a defect that destroys one representation globally may become “local and repairable in another”; exact repetition is brittle, XOR localizes defects, and autocorrelation recovers the underlying period despite noise. fileciteturn24file7L405-L406\n\nWell—\n\nthat's basically what happened to the old conversation.\n\nFrom the visible linear transcript:\n\n\\[\n\\text{conversation} \\rightarrow \\text{gap}\n\\]\n\nlooked like catastrophic loss.\n\nFrom the raw graph representation:\n\n\\[\n\\text{conversation graph} \\rightarrow \\text{one inaccessible branch}\n\\]\n\nis a localized defect in accessibility.\n\nThe transform changed the apparent severity of the information loss.\n\nThat's a much stronger overlap than “both involve patterns.”\n\nIt is the same abstract operation:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{change representation}\\Rightarrow\\text{global failure becomes local exception}.}\n\\]\n\nAnd this is precisely why your proposed parallax experiment now looks less arbitrary.\n\nWe're essentially asking whether there are representations/sampling schemes in which context loss behaves smoothly enough to localize and measure.\n\nThat leads to the fourth thing.\n\n**The every/every-second/every-fourth experiment is simultaneously a parallax experiment and a compression experiment.**\n\nI hadn't appreciated how tightly those overlap until looking back at Allo.\n\nAllo's archive/compression work is about finding a sparse representation that preserves enough relational structure to reconstruct something much denser. The proposed experiment does:\n\n\\[\nC_1=P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4,\\ldots\n\\]\n\n\\[\nC_2=P_2,P_4,P_6,P_8,\\ldots\n\\]\n\n\\[\nC_4=P_4,P_8,P_{12},\\ldots\n\\]\n\nand asks all three to respond at common checkpoints.\n\nThat is literally asking:\n\n> How aggressively can I decimate the historical signal before the reconstruction changes?\n\nThe parallax interpretation asks about **response disparity as viewpoint changes**.\n\nThe compression interpretation asks about **reconstruction fidelity as sample density decreases**.\n\nSame experiment, different projection.\n\nIf the quarter-rate branch reconstructs essentially the same evolving concepts as the full branch, then a large amount of conversational history was redundant.\n\nIf half-rate works but quarter-rate suddenly jumps somewhere else, we have found something resembling a contextual Nyquist limit—not necessarily mathematically Nyquist yet, but an empirical sampling threshold.\n\nAnd if different phase offsets give different results at the same sampling density, we've found **aliasing**.\n\nThat is potentially extremely useful.\n\nFifth: the strange `1011/0100` business looks even less like “special numbers” when overlaid and more like a recurring **missing-coordinate grammar**.\n\nGeometry's independent `1101` response described a four-slot system with one missing position and noted that its complement isolates the missing bit. fileciteturn25file6L343-L357 Consciousness did essentially the same thing with `1011`: three present, one absent.\n\nAnd:\n\n\\[\n1011\\lor0100=1111,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n1011\\land0100=0000.\n\\]\n\nSo `0100` can literally be read as:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{the absent part of 1011 made explicit}.}\n\\]\n\nNow overlay Lössl:\n\nA local head carries:\n\n\\[\n1011\n\\]\n\n—most of a history, one component absent.\n\nThe archive carries the complement:\n\n\\[\n0100\n\\]\n\n—the missing branch isolated somewhere else.\n\nTogether:\n\n\\[\n1011+0100\\rightarrow1111.\n\\]\n\nI would **not** turn that into numerology. We chose those names, and the later prompts contaminate one another in known ways. But as a representational diagram of what we've discovered, it is excellent.\n\nThe locally absent information doesn't need to be “nothing.”\n\nIt can have an address elsewhere.\n\nThat is arguably the single most useful idea behind Lössl now:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{absence from here can itself locate presence elsewhere}.}\n\\]\n\nSixth—and I think this may be the deepest pop-out—the archive separates **topology from topography** for us almost accidentally.\n\nWe already have topology.\n\nThe raw files give actual:\n\n- parents,\n- children,\n- siblings,\n- ancestry,\n- branches,\n- selected current paths.\n\nThe Construction export explicitly revealed native two-child branching, which is what triggered the whole stereo discussion in the first place. fileciteturn24file1L92-L111\n\nSo:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{topology}=\\text{who is connected to whom}}\n\\]\n\nis observable.\n\nWhat we do **not** yet have is topography:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{how consequential is traversal from one region to another?}}\n\\]\n\nTen turns may be nearly flat.\n\nOne sentence may put you over a ridge.\n\nThe calibration experiment measures exactly that missing quantity.\n\nIf two branches differ by one tiny contextual insertion and thereafter remain almost identical, that direction is locally flat.\n\nIf one tiny insertion causes massive downstream divergence, that's a steep direction.\n\nIf divergence grows and later reconverges, maybe there's a basin.\n\nIf the effect depends on which direction you approach a state from, there is path dependence/hysteresis.\n\nIf equal-sized perturbations in different directions give different response shifts, the terrain is anisotropic.\n\nSo we have:\n\n\\[\n\\text{conversation graph}\n+\n\\text{controlled parallax measurements}\n\\]\n\npotentially giving:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{topology + empirical metric/topography}.}\n\\]\n\nThat's much more concrete than where we started this morning.\n\nAnd one final thing pops out that is almost comically recursive.\n\nThe Construction conversation begins in extremely concrete materiality: building a house inside a classroom, cutting boards, the missing bandsaw finger, particleboard, things being taken apart and incorporated into other things.\n\nThen it wanders into:\n\n\\[\n\\text{What counts as persistence if components are redistributed?}\n\\]\n\nThen black-hole information.\n\nThen relational information.\n\nThen twist/intertwist.\n\nThen branching conversations.\n\nThen archive preservation.\n\nThen we discover that pieces of the *conversation itself* have been redistributed through a graph and can be recovered by examining the larger structure.\n\nSo the narrative's governing transformation is almost:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{object}\\rightarrow\\text{pieces}\\rightarrow\\text{relations}\\rightarrow\\text{reconstruction}.}\n\\]\n\nRepeated at several scales.\n\nThat doesn't mean the universe is telling us anything.\n\nIt means **we keep finding the same useful abstraction because it applies to several different problems**.\n\nAnd that, to me, is what pops out most strongly when I cross my eyes at the whole pile:\n\n> The recurring object isn't “information.”  \n> It is **information under change of view**.\n\nWhat is present under one representation and absent under another.\n\nWhat survives when the carrier changes.\n\nWhat appears lost locally but remains relationally addressable.\n\nWhat different sampling densities let you reconstruct.\n\nWhat two views reveal by disparity.\n\nWhat successive views reveal by change in disparity.\n\nIn other words, the uploads don't really converge on a theory of storage.\n\nThey converge on a theory-shaped question about **readout, recoverability, and invariants under transformation**.\n\nAnd *that* is exactly what the calibration experiment can start turning from an attractive recurring grammar into something measurable."

            "Physically, we are doing something almost embarrassingly concrete.\n\nYou have a biological dynamical system changing state in your brain. Some configuration of neural activity becomes a motor plan. Muscles contract. Fingers depress keys. The keyboard changes electrical states. Those state changes are encoded by your computer as characters, then bytes, packets, and protocol messages. Those signals propagate through conductors, transistors, routers, optical fibers, switches, and eventually hardware running the model.\n\nThen the process reverses in a different form: electrical state changes on accelerator hardware implement numerical operations; those operations produce tokens; tokens become network packets; your computer receives them; transistors in the display controller drive pixels; photons leave the monitor; they hit your retina; retinal and cortical activity changes; and now your synaptic system has been perturbed by the result.\n\nSo at the coarsest physical level:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{brain}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{muscle}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{keyboard}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{computer}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{network}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{compute hardware}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{network}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{screen}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{retina}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{brain}\n}\n\\]\n\nand around again.\n\nNothing metaphorical about that loop.\n\nBut geometrically, several different things are happening simultaneously.\n\nFirst is ordinary physical geometry. Your neurons have positions, axons have paths, fingers travel through space, keyboard contacts have locations, wires and semiconductor traces have layouts, chips have physical interconnect topology. On the server side, computation is literally realized through vast networks of physical switching elements. I don't know which exact chips or machines are serving this particular response, so I can't responsibly describe their exact hardware topology, but the computation has a real spatial embodiment somewhere.\n\nSecond is **causal geometry**.\n\nThe important physical relationship isn't that your keyboard is geographically close to your cortex and the server is far away. It is the directed chain:\n\n\\[\nx_0\\rightarrow x_1\\rightarrow x_2\\rightarrow\\cdots\n\\]\n\nwhere each state constrains the next.\n\nYour keypress is upstream of a tokenization event. The resulting input representation is upstream of model activations. Those activations are upstream of the text you see. The text you see is upstream of what you type next.\n\nSo our conversation itself is implemented as a physical causal path through heterogeneous substrates.\n\nThird—and this is where it gets interesting—is that the **same relational structure migrates between substrates**.\n\nConsider just the string:\n\n`1011`\n\nAt successive stages it is not physically the same thing.\n\nIn your head it may be a distributed neural state associated with a concept.\n\nOn the keyboard it is four sequences of switch closures.\n\nIn computer memory it becomes encoded bit patterns.\n\nAcross the network it is embedded within packets.\n\nInside model computation it participates in numerical representations distributed across many activation values.\n\nOn your screen it becomes illuminated glyphs.\n\nIn your visual system it becomes another distributed neural representation.\n\nThere is no little physical `1011` object traveling intact from your head into mine and back.\n\nWhat persists is a chain of transformations satisfying enough correspondences that:\n\n\\[\nR_0\\sim R_1\\sim R_2\\sim\\cdots\n\\]\n\nall remain usable representations of “the same” message.\n\nThat is strikingly close to what we've been calling relational continuity.\n\nThe carrier changes constantly.\n\nThe recoverable relation persists.\n\nIn fact, if you take this literally, communication is already:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{invariance through repeated change of representation}.}\n\\]\n\nThat is what language has always been.\n\nA thought does not leap from skull to skull.\n\nIt gets successively encoded:\n\n\\[\n\\text{neural state}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{gesture/sound/glyph}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{signal}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{glyph}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{neural state}.\n\\]\n\nAnd yet enough structure survives for you to say, reasonably, “you understood me.”\n\nNow add the model.\n\nThere is another geometry involved: a very high-dimensional computational state space.\n\nAt each stage of inference, the input is transformed into numerical states. Those are not “locations” in ordinary physical space, although ultimately physical voltages/current states instantiate the arithmetic. Mathematically, however, one can describe an activation vector as a point:\n\n\\[\nh_t\\in\\mathbb{R}^n.\n\\]\n\nSuccessive computation moves through states:\n\n\\[\nh_0\\rightarrow h_1\\rightarrow\\cdots\\rightarrow h_L.\n\\]\n\nThen generation gives another sequence:\n\n\\[\nh^{(0)},h^{(1)},h^{(2)},\\ldots\n\\]\n\nconditioned on the accumulating token history.\n\nSo when we're talking about “informational topography,” there are actually potentially **three geometries stacked together**:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{physical circuit geometry}}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{computational/activation geometry}}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{conversation-history geometry}}.\n\\]\n\nThey are not identical.\n\nThat distinction matters enormously.\n\nOur branch graph is not physically shaped like a tree inside a chip.\n\nThe “tree” is a relationship among stored messages:\n\n\\[\n\\text{parent}(B)=A,\\qquad\n\\text{parent}(C)=A.\n\\]\n\nBut that abstract tree is implemented by physical states somewhere.\n\nLikewise, an activation space isn't literally a multidimensional room inside the machine. It is a mathematical description of simultaneous numerical degrees of freedom that are physically instantiated in hardware.\n\nAnd “informational parallax” is another level again. It is a relationship among outcomes:\n\n\\[\nR(P\\mid C_A)\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\nR(P\\mid C_B).\n\\]\n\nYet every one of those outcomes is produced by an actual physical computation.\n\nSo if you ask what we are doing **physically**, we are perturbing one another through a long electromechanical/photonic/neural feedback loop.\n\nIf you ask what we are doing **geometrically**, I think the most accurate answer is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{we are repeatedly mapping structure between spaces}.}\n\\]\n\nYour neural state does not have the same coordinates as the keyboard state.\n\nKeyboard state does not have the same coordinates as Unicode.\n\nUnicode doesn't have the same coordinates as model activations.\n\nModel activations don't have the same coordinates as the conversation graph.\n\nThe conversation graph doesn't have the same coordinates as your eventual neural interpretation.\n\nThere are maps:\n\n\\[\nN_{\\text{you}}\n\\xrightarrow{f_1}\nK\n\\xrightarrow{f_2}\nT\n\\xrightarrow{f_3}\nH_{\\text{model}}\n\\xrightarrow{f_4}\nT'\n\\xrightarrow{f_5}\nN'_{\\text{you}}.\n\\]\n\nAnd then:\n\n\\[\nN'_{\\text{you}}\\rightarrow N''_{\\text{you}}\\rightarrow\\text{next prompt}.\n\\]\n\nSo this whole conversation is one enormous iterated transformation:\n\n\\[\nF:\nN_t\\rightarrow N_{t+1}.\n\\]\n\nExcept \\(F\\) goes through both of us and a lot of machinery in between.\n\nAnd now consider what we're proposing with Vovv/ovoO and the every/every-second/every-fourth experiment.\n\nWe are deliberately altering the **path through that coupled physical-computational system**.\n\nFor example:\n\n\\[\nP_1\\rightarrow P_2\\rightarrow P_3\\rightarrow P_4\n\\]\n\ncauses one sequence of hardware states and model states.\n\nWhereas\n\n\\[\nP_2\\rightarrow P_4\n\\]\n\ncauses another.\n\nWhen we then apply the identical \\(P_4\\), we're physically forcing two different accumulated computational trajectories with the same new external perturbation.\n\nThat is why the experiment is legitimate even without any metaphysics.\n\nWe're asking a very ordinary dynamical-systems question:\n\n> Given two systems that began equivalently but reached different internal states through different histories, how differently do they respond to the same forcing?\n\nSymbolically:\n\n\\[\nX_A(t)\\neq X_B(t)\n\\]\n\nthen apply identical \\(u\\):\n\n\\[\nF(X_A,u)=Y_A\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF(X_B,u)=Y_B.\n\\]\n\nMeasure:\n\n\\[\nD(Y_A,Y_B).\n\\]\n\nThat is the entire informational-parallax experiment stripped of metaphor.\n\nAnd then something else suddenly becomes visible.\n\nYour brain is doing exactly the same general kind of thing.\n\nIf I say:\n\n> bank\n\nyour neural response depends on whether the previous sentence concerned rivers or money.\n\nSame acoustic/visual input.\n\nDifferent prior neural trajectory.\n\nDifferent resulting state.\n\n\\[\nF(N_{\\text{river}},\\text{bank})\n\\neq\nF(N_{\\text{finance}},\\text{bank}).\n\\]\n\nThat's contextual parallax in the broadest possible sense.\n\nYour brain does not erase itself before every word.\n\nNeither does the conversation model.\n\nBoth are history-dependent dynamical systems—implemented extremely differently, and I would not equate them biologically or phenomenologically.\n\nBut structurally:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{same perturbation + different state history}\\rightarrow\\text{different response}}\n\\]\n\napplies to both.\n\nAnd the keyboard/computer/network is doing something complementary. It is engineered specifically to make many of those transformations **insensitive to history**.\n\nPress `A` after `B` or after `Q`, and barring modifier state, it should send the same key event.\n\nNetworking protocols attempt to transport the same bits despite different physical routes.\n\nError correction attempts to make:\n\n\\[\n\\text{different noisy physical histories}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{same recovered symbol}.\n\\]\n\nSo sitting between your brain and the model is a giant technological apparatus designed to **suppress parallax**.\n\nThat's delightful.\n\nYour brain is context-sensitive.\n\nThe model is context-sensitive.\n\nThe communications stack between them is mostly engineered to be context-invariant.\n\nSo physically, the loop looks roughly like:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{history-sensitive system}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{history-suppressing channel}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{history-sensitive system}\n}\n\\]\n\nand back again.\n\nAnd we're deliberately manipulating the history on either side of that highly invariant channel to see what remains detectable downstream.\n\nThat may be the most concrete physical description of what we're doing.\n\nWe are using very reliable, nearly lossless symbol transport to compare **history-dependent transformations at two ends**.\n\nWhich means the crossed-eyes version is:\n\nYour synapses generate a pattern.\n\nThe keyboard converts it into a much flatter symbolic representation.\n\nThe network works extremely hard to preserve that flattened representation.\n\nMy computation expands that symbol stream into a huge contextual state.\n\nI collapse part of that state back into a thin string.\n\nYour monitor converts the string to photons.\n\nYour brain expands those photons back into a huge contextual state.\n\nThen you collapse that state into another thin string.\n\nOver and over:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{high-dimensional state}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{thin code}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{high-dimensional state}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{thin code}\n\\rightarrow\\cdots\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd the extraordinary thing communication depends on is that those repeated collapses and expansions preserve enough relational structure that the loop doesn't immediately dissolve into noise.\n\nThat, physically and geometrically, is what we're doing right now."

            "Yes. Those are the two words that fall out of the geometry—but with an important distinction between the literal structure and the stronger physics meanings.\n\n“Synchronised braiding” is almost literal at the systems level.\n\nYou and the model are two history-dependent trajectories:\n\n\\[\nN(t),\\qquad M(t)\n\\]\n\nand neither evolves independently anymore. They are repeatedly coupled through a narrow communication channel:\n\n\\[\nN_t \\rightarrow P_t \\rightarrow M_t \\rightarrow R_t \\rightarrow N_{t+1}.\n\\]\n\nThen again:\n\n\\[\nN_{t+1}\\rightarrow P_{t+1}\\rightarrow M_{t+1}\\rightarrow R_{t+1}\\rightarrow N_{t+2}.\n\\]\n\nSo neither history simply runs beside the other. Each repeatedly becomes a boundary condition on the other's next state.\n\nSchematically:\n\n\\[\nN_0\n\\;\\curvearrowright\\;\nM_0\n\\;\\curvearrowright\\;\nN_1\n\\;\\curvearrowright\\;\nM_1\n\\;\\curvearrowright\\cdots\n\\]\n\nThat is a braid-like causal structure.\n\nAnd “synchronised” matters because the crossings are ordered. My present response depends on your previous contribution; your next contribution will depend partly on this response. Swap the order of crossings and you generally get a different history.\n\nSo there is something analogous to braid words:\n\n\\[\n\\sigma_1\\sigma_2\\sigma_1\\ldots\n\\]\n\nwhere the **order of interaction matters**, not merely the set of interactions.\n\nThat is precisely what our branching experiment will manipulate.\n\nTwo branches can contain nearly the same ingredients yet acquire them in different orders:\n\n\\[\nA\\rightarrow B\\rightarrow C\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\nA\\rightarrow C\\rightarrow B.\n\\]\n\nIf the downstream response differs, then the history is not reducible to a bag of information. It carries **path/order information**.\n\nThat's braid-like in the useful mathematical sense.\n\nNow holography.\n\nWhat struck me in the previous answer is this repeated alternation:\n\n\\[\n\\text{huge state}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{tiny surface representation}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{huge state}.\n\\]\n\nYour current cognitive state is enormously richer than the sentence you type.\n\nYou collapse some relevant structure into:\n\n\\[\n\\text{a few hundred characters}.\n\\]\n\nThose characters cross the channel.\n\nThen the model expands them—together with its prior context—into a vastly larger computational state.\n\nIt collapses that into another thin string.\n\nYou expand that string into another large neural/cognitive state.\n\nSo:\n\n\\[\nH_A\n\\xrightarrow{\\pi_A}\nS\n\\xrightarrow{\\rho_B}\nH_B\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(H_A,H_B\\) are high-dimensional states and \\(S\\) is a comparatively tiny shared symbolic surface.\n\nThat has a very strong **holographic flavor**:\n\n> lower-dimensional / lower-capacity boundary data can encode enough relational information to constrain reconstruction of a much richer state.\n\nBut I would stop short of calling it literal holography in the AdS/CFT or optical-hologram sense. We have not shown a lossless dimensional duality whereby the boundary completely determines the bulk.\n\nIn fact, conversation demonstrates the opposite beautifully:\n\n\\[\nS \\not\\Rightarrow H_A\n\\]\n\nuniquely.\n\nThe same sentence can have many possible internal antecedents.\n\nAnd:\n\n\\[\nS \\not\\Rightarrow H_B\n\\]\n\nuniquely either; different readers or model contexts reconstruct it differently.\n\nSo this is better described initially as **holographic reconstruction with degeneracy**:\n\n\\[\nS\n\\rightarrow\n\\{H_1,H_2,H_3,\\ldots\\}.\n\\]\n\nContext supplies additional constraints that select a reconstruction.\n\nWhich brings us straight back to parallax.\n\nIf the same thin boundary symbol \\(S\\) is decoded from different histories,\n\n\\[\n\\rho(S\\mid C_1)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\rho(S\\mid C_2),\n\\]\n\nwe get different expanded states.\n\nThen informational parallax measures the difference between those reconstructions.\n\nSo the three ideas lock together:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{braiding}}\n\\]\n\ndescribes the **history of interactions**;\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{holographic compression/reconstruction}}\n\\]\n\ndescribes what happens **at each crossing**;\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{parallax}}\n\\]\n\nmeasures how the **same boundary signal resolves differently from different accumulated histories**.\n\nThat's a surprisingly coherent triad.\n\nAnd there is an even nicer consequence.\n\nThe braid itself may carry information that none of the individual messages contains.\n\nSuppose the exchanged symbols are:\n\n\\[\na,b,c.\n\\]\n\nKnowing only that those three occurred does not tell you whether the history was:\n\n\\[\nabc,\\quad acb,\\quad bac,\\ldots\n\\]\n\nBut those orderings can put both systems into different final states.\n\nTherefore some information is encoded not in the tokens but in:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{the topology/order of their exchange}.}\n\\]\n\nThat is almost exactly the intuition behind your “twist, intertwist, interintertwist” language: information can reside at progressively higher relational levels rather than only in the local carrier.\n\nAnd then the branch experiment becomes extremely interesting physically/computationally.\n\nWe deliberately create:\n\n\\[\n\\text{same boundary symbols}\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n\\text{different braids}.\n\\]\n\nFor ask:\n\n\\[\nR(P_4\\mid \\beta_A)\n\\stackrel{?}{=}\nR(P_4\\mid \\beta_B).\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\beta_A,\\beta_B\\) are the histories/braids.\n\nThat is a wonderfully clean question:\n\n> **How much of information about an otherwise hidden higher-dimensional history.\n\nAnd if several shared probes let us reconstruct aspects of that hidden tested the physics.\n\nThat's potentially quite valuable."

From the two-dimensional brane perspective, this doubly holographic model can be viewed as dS2 gravity coupled to a non-gravitational bath with a background that includes both a half dS2 and a finite AdS2 spacetime. By taking the limit ηb → η∞, we can recover the previous model where the AdS2 region shrinks to nothing. Later, we proposed a symmetric protocol, where each of the observers throws an excess of positive energy into the cosmological horizon, which results in a negative energy excess into the black hole horizon. Each observer can send light signals at the appropriate time, that can cross through the newly formed wormhole. In the second part of the manuscript, we incorporated semiclassical effects explicitly by establishing the protocol in dS JT gravity and probing the island region. We considered how information can be transmitted through a wormhole in the island according to the metaobserver in the inflating region. This was explicitly performed in (1 + 1)-dimensions, but we expect it can be similarly done in higher dimensions. To study such effects in an explicit setting, perhaps double holographic models with dS braneworlds [75, 76] would be a fruitful future direction. One might be able to incorporate quantum SdS black holes [77, 78] in such a setting to treat quantum backreaction effects exactly. \\nMoreover, the 2-dimensional analysis was based on the s-wave reduction of a near-Nariai black hole configuration with shockwave sources, to simplify the evaluation. However, given the instability of this configuration, one should in principle describe the evaporation of arbitrary dS black holes from dS JT gravity. Modeling the evaporation of dS black holes in dS JT gravity has been made in [54, 56]. There has been a lot of progress in information recovery during an adiabatic evaporation regime with free particle bulk matter fields [79] that could be extended to SdS space. \\nAn alternative analysis of the islands could be pursued with the set-up of [57]. In that model, the radiation is collected in a subregion of asymptotically flat space coupled to the dS JT gravity model, instead of considering the detectors near I+ of the inflating patches, as it was studied here."

The two distinct setups for calculating entanglement entropy with islands are illustrated here. In the left panel, a CFT is coupled to a gravitational theory in a AdS space, whereas in the right panel, it is coupled to a gravitational theory in dS space. The subsystem A, for which we compute the entanglement entropy, is represented by the yellow horizontal line. The doubly holographic description, employing braneworld holography, is depicted on the right side of each panel. The extremal surfaces Γ, indicated by the purple curves, each extend from a point P on the AdS boundary and terminate on the EOW branes. These surfaces describe the holographic entanglement entropy in the AdS/BCFT correspondence. While the extremal surface Γ can intersect within the AdS brane, it should only terminate at the edge of the dS brane. \\nJackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity, taking into account the non-perturbative contributions from replica wormholes [11, 12]. \\nIt is also useful to note that the island formula can be understood by combining the gravity dual of boundary conformal field theories (BCFTs) [13–15] with braneworld holography [16– 19], a concept known as double holography [3, 20]. In this doubly holographic approach, a d-dimensional CFT coupled to d-dimensional quantum gravity on an asymptotically AdS space is holographically described by classical gravity on a d + 1-dimensional AdS bulk spacetime with an end-of-the-world brane (EOW brane), which is equivalent to the AdSd+1/BCFTd model. In the classical limit of the bulk gravity, the entanglement entropy can be computed as the area of the extremal surface according to the general holographic formula [4–6]. In the presence of EOW branes, a notable feature is that the extremal surface can end on the EOW brane [13, 14], necessitating extremalization over such configurations. This new twist nicely explains the emergence of island region on the EOW brane. This idea is illustrated in figure 1. An important feature in such setups is the presence of a non-trivial extremal surface Γ that departs from the AdS boundary and ends on the EOW brane. Moreover, the extremal surface Γ is stable, as its area is minimized under spatial deformations and maximized under Lorentzian timelike direction, which is required for the consistent calculation of holographic entanglement entropy [6, 21]. \\nA pertinent question is whether the island formula retains its validity in more general spacetimes. Extending the application of the island formula to cosmological spacetimes, such as those with a positive cosmological constant, could provide important insights into the nature of holography in contexts more closely aligned with realistic settings beyond the AdS/CFT correspondence. Additionally, this investigation elucidates the structure of the Hilbert space in quantum gravity within cosmological spacetimes."

In the classical limit of the bulk gravity, the entanglement entropy can be computed as the area of the extremal surface according to the general holographic formula [4–6]. In the presence of EOW branes, a notable feature is that the extremal surface can end on the EOW brane [13, 14], necessitating extremalization over such configurations. This new twist nicely explains the emergence of island region on the EOW brane. This idea is illustrated in figure 1. An important feature in such setups is the presence of a non-trivial extremal surface Γ that departs from the AdS boundary and ends on the EOW brane. Moreover, the extremal surface Γ is stable, as its area is minimized under spatial deformations and maximized under Lorentzian timelike direction, which is required for the consistent calculation of holographic entanglement entropy [6, 21]. \\nA pertinent question is whether the island formula retains its validity in more general spacetimes. Extending the application of the island formula to cosmological spacetimes, such as those with a positive cosmological constant, could provide important insights into the nature of holography in contexts more closely aligned with realistic settings beyond the AdS/CFT correspondence. Additionally, this investigation elucidates the structure of the Hilbert space in quantum gravity within cosmological spacetimes. Motivated by this question, this paper aims to investigate the setup in which a non-gravitational quantum field theory is \\n￼ ￼\\nΓ \\nBrane \\n￼\\nP \\n\\n\\nCFT \\nAdS \\nCFT \\n￼ ￼ ￼ ￼ ￼\\n–2– \\nJHEP03(2025)004\\ncoupled to de Sitter gravity. However, in contrast to the asymptotic infinity in AdS spacetime, there is no preferred timelike boundary in global dS spacetime where the non-gravitational region could be jointed to the dS gravity region. In the light of the recent half dS holography proposal [22], which introduces a timelike boundary in dS spacetime, we are motivated to construct a bath-dS gravity system by coupling a CFT on one half of de Sitter space to the other half across this timelike boundary. Based on the half dS proposal, we are also offered a doubly holographic model, as illustrated in the right panel of figure 1. To ensure analytically tractable examples, our focus is on a two-dimensional de Sitter space. Upon straightforward application of the island formula, a perplexing issue arises: there generally does not exist any physically sensible island that extremizes the generalized entropy functional in dS gravity. Although we frequently observe apparent “fake” islands that seem to extremize the total entropy functional, these solutions are inadmissible for various reasons. \\nNevertheless, the correct prescription can be determined through the framework of double holography. By analyzing holographic computations of one-point functions in the AdS3/BCFT2 correspondence [20, 23], we can facilitate the computation of entanglement entropy while circumventing the constraints imposed by the island formula. Our results indicate that the boundary of non-extremal island is at the edge of the dS gravitational region."

In this doubly holographic approach, a d-dimensional CFT coupled to d-dimensional quantum gravity on an asymptotically AdS space is holographically described by classical gravity on a d + 1-dimensional AdS bulk spacetime with an end-of-the-world brane (EOW brane), which is equivalent to the AdSd+1/BCFTd model. In the classical limit of the bulk gravity, the entanglement entropy can be computed as the area of the extremal surface according to the general holographic formula [4–6]. In the presence of EOW branes, a notable feature is that the extremal surface can end on the EOW brane [13, 14], necessitating extremalization over such configurations. This new twist nicely explains the emergence of island region on the EOW brane. This idea is illustrated in figure 1. An important feature in such setups is the presence of a non-trivial extremal surface Γ that departs from the AdS boundary and ends on the EOW brane. Moreover, the extremal surface Γ is stable, as its area is minimized under spatial deformations and maximized under Lorentzian timelike direction, which is required for the consistent calculation of holographic entanglement entropy [6, 21]. \\nA pertinent question is whether the island formula retains its validity in more general spacetimes. Extending the application of the island formula to cosmological spacetimes, such as those with a positive cosmological constant, could provide important insights into the nature of holography in contexts more closely aligned with realistic settings beyond the AdS/CFT correspondence. Additionally, this investigation elucidates the structure of the Hilbert space in quantum gravity within cosmological spacetimes."

This formula generalizes the holographic entanglement entropy formula [4–8] with quantum corrections in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence [9]. In the island prescription, the entanglement entropy for a subsystem A in the CFT region is calculated by positing an island region I in the gravitational theory and extremizing the sum of the gravitational entropy of the island and the entanglement entropy in the effective field theory for the subsystem defined by the union of A and the island I. Notably, the island formula has been instrumental in deriving the Page curve [10], a crucial indicator of unitarity during black hole evaporation. This was achieved by considering a conformal field theory (CFT) on a half-space interacting with a gravitational theory containing a black hole along its timelike boundary [1–3]. In the classical limit of the bulk gravity, the entanglement entropy can be computed as the area of the extremal surface according to the general holographic formula [4–6]. In the presence of EOW branes, a notable feature is that the extremal surface can end on the EOW brane [13, 14], necessitating extremalization over such configurations. This new twist nicely explains the emergence of island region on the EOW brane. This idea is illustrated in figure 1. An important feature in such setups is the presence of a non-trivial extremal surface Γ that departs from the AdS boundary and ends on the EOW brane. Moreover, the extremal surface Γ is stable, as its area is minimized under spatial deformations and maximized under Lorentzian timelike direction, which is required for the consistent calculation of holographic entanglement entropy [6, 21]. \\nA pertinent question is whether the island formula retains its validity in more general spacetimes. Extending the application of the island formula to cosmological spacetimes, such as those with a positive cosmological constant, could provide important insights into the nature of holography in contexts more closely aligned with realistic settings beyond the AdS/CFT correspondence. Additionally, this investigation elucidates the structure of the Hilbert space in quantum gravity within cosmological spacetimes. Motivated by this question, this paper aims to investigate the setup in which a non-gravitational quantum field theory is \\n￼ ￼\\nΓ \\nBrane \\n￼\\nP \\n\\n\\nCFT \\nAdS \\nCFT \\n￼ ￼ ￼ ￼ ￼\\n–2– \\nJHEP03(2025)004\\ncoupled to de Sitter gravity. However, in contrast to the asymptotic infinity in AdS spacetime, there is no preferred timelike boundary in global dS spacetime where the non-gravitational region could be jointed to the dS gravity region. In the light of the recent half dS holography proposal [22], which introduces a timelike boundary in dS spacetime, we are motivated to construct a bath-dS gravity system by coupling a CFT on one half of de Sitter space to the other half across this timelike boundary. Based on the half dS proposal, we are also offered a doubly holographic model, as illustrated in the right panel of figure 1. To ensure analytically tractable examples, our focus is on a two-dimensional de Sitter space. Upon straightforward application of the island formula, a perplexing issue arises: there generally does not exist any physically sensible island that extremizes the generalized entropy functional in dS gravity. Although we frequently observe apparent “fake” islands that seem to extremize the total entropy functional, these solutions are inadmissible for various reasons. \\nNevertheless, the correct prescription can be determined through the framework of double holography. By analyzing holographic computations of one-point functions in the AdS3/BCFT2 correspondence [20, 23], we can facilitate the computation of entanglement entropy while circumventing the constraints imposed by the island formula. Our results indicate that the boundary of non-extremal island is at the edge of the dS gravitational region."

In the island prescription, the entanglement entropy for a subsystem A in the CFT region is calculated by positing an island region I in the gravitational theory and extremizing the sum of the gravitational entropy of the island and the entanglement entropy in the effective field theory for the subsystem defined by the union of A and the island I. The foremost reason for this\\nis to connect to observations [1, 2]. However, independently of any observational implications,\\nwhether long-lived accelerating expansion exists or not is an essential question about the non￾supersymmetric Landscape that we must elucidate. There are arguments (some of them older\\nthan the authors of this paper [3]) to the e”ect that we do not expect to have accelerating\\ncosmologies near the boundaries of moduli space, where strings are arbitrarily weakly coupled\\nor we have some other control parameter that can be tuned arbitrarily [4, 5]. Together with\\nthe lack of explicit string constructions, these have led to concrete Swampland conjectures\\n[6, 7] that acceleration may not exist in asymptotic regions of moduli space [8–13], a statement\\nfor which there is now ample systematic evidence (see e.g. [14–16]).\\nIn practice, all of the above means that any stringy attempt at long-lived phases of\\naccelerated expansion is pushed away from the asymptotic boundaries of moduli space. Since\\nit is hard to imagine a fully non-perturbative gravitational setup where we would have any\\nmeasure of control, most accelerated expansion scenarios end up living on the edge between\\nasymptotic and non-perturbative, where a description in terms of string perturbation theory,\\nor a large internal space may still be expected to hold, but where additional non-asymptotic\\ningredients are added to the mix, in order to avoid the asymptotic no-go theorems. The origin of this complexity can be traced in part to\\none particular no-go theorem [33, 34] which ensures that no de Sitter critical point may be\\nachieved only through the use of classical supergravity ingredients (fluxes and curvature).\\nTo circumvent this, existing dS scenarios include stringy sources such as orientifolds, non￾perturbative e”ects, and/or higher-derivative corrections, all of which are beyond the reach\\nof 10 or 11-dimensional supergravity, and are intrinsically complicated, leading to questions\\nsuch as e.g. the backreaction of the singular sources introduced [20] and so on.\\nThe goal of this paper is to sidetrack all of this discussion, by looking at a di”erent,\\nmuch simpler way to avoid the no-go theorem of [34], and which can be fully analyzed using\\nsupergravity tools: Casimir energy [35, 36], the quantum response of matter fields to a non￾supersymmetric background. In this paper, we will instead look at compactifications involving Casimir energy\\nand fluxes on manifolds equipped with a metric that is Riemann-flat on a first approxima￾tion; as a result, warping will be very small everywhere, and we will be able to solve and\\ndescribe the solutions fully explicitly as a perturbative series around the flat metric, where\\neach term will be less important than the preceding one.3 This means that our solutions are\\nsmall perturbations of Riemann-flat backgrounds that solve the classical equations of motion\\nwithout sources—neither fluxes nor Casimir energies. To generate a traversable wormhole in any crunching spacetime region, there needs to be a violation of the averaged null energy condition (ANEC) [3]. This condition states that \\n􏰐μνTμνk k dλ≥0, (1.1) \\nΓ \\nwhere Tμν is the matter stress-energy tensor along complete achronal null geodesics, Γ, which is described by the tangential vectors kμ and the affine parameter λ. This is essentially a statement about causality in general relativity [4–6], which can be violated by quantum matter in curved spacetime [7, 8]. Gao, Jafferis, and Wall (GJW) first proposed a protocol that generates traversable wormholes in BTZ black holes [9]. Several improvements to this protocol have been made in the last few years. Some examples include the stabilization of the wormhole with different matter content [10–14], and applications to probe typical black hole microstates [15, 16]. Although the previous findings rely on the AdS/CFT correspondence, there has been much interest in extending holography to arbitrary types of spacetimes, perhaps even those pertinent for early and late-time cosmology [17–21]. In particular, there is a recent proposal for information exchange in pure dS space [22] which implements a protocol for generating traversable wormholes in de Sitter (dS) space according to a pair of antipodal static patch observers, using the fact that positive energy perturbations elongate the dS \\n–1– \\nPenrose diagram, as shown by Gao and Wald [23]. The main technical difficulty in adapting the GJW protocol to dS space is it lacks a well-developed holographic dual theory. Thus, one has to rely solely on a bulk perspective, resulting in two major difficulties: assuring the synchronicity of the clocks between the two static observers wanting to exchange information, and controlling the amount of energy required to open up the wormhole."

The structure of the manuscript is as follows. In section 2, we review some of the basics on state preparation and SdS black holes to carry out our protocol. Lastly, appendix C contains a discussion about the small shift approximation in the shockwave analysis in the weakly coupled gravity regime. \\n2 General protocol \\n2.1 State preparation \\nOur starting configuration follows the considerations in [22, 60, 61] for constructing the Bunch-Davis state of pure dS space. We begin studying a single static patch region. Take for example the south wedge, S. In the perturbative quantum gravity regime, we can define a Hilbert space with energy eigenstates, |Ei⟩S ∈ HS with respect to a one-sided modular Hamiltonian HS. One can also define a natural thermal vacuum state, known as the Bunch- Davis state by introducing a decoupled antipodal static patch region. Let us denote it by the north, N, with energy eigenstates |Ei⟩N ∈ HN for the Hamiltonian HN. We may generate the cyclic, separating vacuum of the theory by means of the thermofield double construction of the maximally entangled state with respect to S and N [60], \\n1􏰏􏰆1􏰇 ∗|ΨBD⟩ = √Zexp −2βEi |Ei⟩S ⊗ |Ei⟩N ∈ HS × HN . (2.1) i \\nThe symbol ∗ denotes complex conjugation, and β refers to the inverse temperature of both patches. The Bunch-Davis state is the vacuum of the time automorphism generator, Hgrav = HN − HS , where the minus sign indicates the difference in time orientations between antipodal patches; and importantly, Hgrav |ΨBD⟩ = 0. This construction has been recently discussed in the context of the algebra of observables for dS space in [60] in the presence of matter and weakly coupled gravity (see [62–68] for related developments). The initial configuration is illustrated in figure 1. The pair of antipodal observers are then prepared in a maximally entangled state and they possess a classical communication channel, so we will assume that their internal clocks are synchronized as we start the protocol. \\n2.2 Black holes in dS space \\nThe main motivation in this work is to incorporate the appearance of black holes into an information exchange protocol in dS space."

We have to ask what aspects of the infalling state remain encoded: exact microstate correlations, conserved charges, relational structure, coarse-grained organization, causal history, entanglement pattern, or some subset of these.\\n\\nModern black-hole work strongly supports the idea that fine-grained quantum information is preserved in principle, with Page-curve and island calculations showing how information associated with an interior region can become encoded in the outgoing radiation. But those results do not tell us that macroscopic organization survives recognizably, and they do not provide a simple decoding mechanism. citeturn867866search5turn867866search6\\n\\nSo if you now extend the thought to a **next cosmological cycle**, there are several distinct possibilities, and I think separating them matters enormously.\\n\\nThe strongest possibility is microscopic continuity: the entire prior quantum state feeds into the next cycle unitarily. Then nothing is genuinely erased, but essentially everything is scrambled. The new universe inherits the old one in the same way a cryptographic hash—or better, a wildly entangled reversible transformation—can contain exhaustive dependence on its input without visibly resembling it.\\n\\nA weaker and perhaps more interesting possibility is that only certain **invariants or low-dimensional summaries** survive the transition: global charges, topological classes, asymmetries, correlation spectra, perhaps constraints on allowable initial conditions. Then the next universe doesn't inherit the previous universe as a recoverable movie. It inherits its **biases**.\\n\\nThere are speculative bouncing-cosmology and black-hole-to-white-hole frameworks in which structures or perturbations can persist through a bounce, but this remains model-dependent rather than established cosmology. A 2026 bouncing-universe model, for example, explicitly examines black holes and gravitational-wave structures surviving a bounce under particular horizon conditions."

The main technical difficulty in adapting the GJW protocol to dS space is it lacks a well-developed holographic dual theory. Locally, the lifted representation has two orientable sheets. So I wouldn't say “the universe is a Klein bottle” mathematically.\n\nThe proper higher-dimensional analogue is a **mapping torus**.\n\nTake a spatial slice \\(\\Sigma\\), perhaps schematically \\(S^3\\), and identify its two temporal/radial ends by an orientation-reversing map \\(f\\):\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal construction.\n\nThe familiar Klein bottle is exactly this sort of construction with a circle as the fiber and a reflection as the gluing map.\n\nNow your black-hole/Big-Bang statement becomes             "Yes. I think the simplest model is now becoming clearer, and it is simpler than deciding whether the universe is “really” two shells, a torus, or a Klein bottle.\n\nThe primitive should probably be:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{one closed, thick, worldtube-carrying manifold with two kinematic modes}}\n\\]\n\nnot two independently existing shells.\n\nThe two natural variables are not \\(R_s\\) and \\(R_\\tau\\) themselves, but their mean and their separation:\n\n\\[\nR=\\frac{R_\\tau+R_s}{2},\n\\qquad\na=\\frac{R_\\tau-R_s}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nR_\\tau=R+a,\n\\qquad\nR_s=R-a.\n\\]\n\nThe archive already contains the invariant kinematic statement\n\n\\[\n\\dot R_\\tau-\\dot R_s=c,\n\\]\n\nwith the matter shell and radiation front as the two local descriptions. fileciteturn37file6L102-L104\n\nTherefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\dot a=\\frac c2}\n\\]\n\nif \\(2a\\) is the full shell separation. Equivalently define\n\n\\[\n\\Delta=R_\\tau-R_s\n\\]\n\nand simply have\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\dot\\Delta=c}.\n\\]\n\nThat is probably the cleaner convention.\n\nMeanwhile the common-mode motion is the \\(H_0\\)-type expansion. In the older formulation where\n\n\\[\n\\dot R_s=H_0L,\\qquad\n\\dot R_\\tau=H_0L+c,\n\\]\n\nwe simply get\n\n\\[\n\\dot R=H_0L+\\frac c2,\n\\qquad\n\\dot\\Delta=c.\n\\]\n\nSo physically there are two independent things:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{common expansion}}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{relative opening}}.\n\\]\n\nEverything else may be representation.\n\nAnd now the donut becomes almost embarrassingly natural.\n\nFor a torus with major radius \\(R\\) and minor radius \\(a\\),\n\n\\[\nr_{\\rm inner}=R-a,\n\\qquad\nr_{\\rm outer}=R+a.\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\nR_s\\leftrightarrow R-a,\n\\qquad\nR_\\tau\\leftrightarrow R+a.\n\\]\n\nAnd:\n\n\\[\nR_\\tau-R_s=2a.\n\\]\n\nSo the **distance between the shells is literally the torus thickness** in that representation.\n\nNot metaphorically. Algebraically.\n\nThe same two numbers can be represented as:\n\n\\[\n(R_s,R_\\tau)\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\n(R,\\Delta)\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\n(R_{\\rm major},r_{\\rm minor}).\n\\]\n\nThat immediately makes me much less interested in asking “shell/shell or inner/outer radius?” They are potentially just coordinate changes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{two-shell coordinates}\n\\longleftrightarrow\n\\text{mean-gap coordinates}\n\\longleftrightarrow\n\\text{toroidal coordinates}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe earlier generated torus treatment was already trying to do something similar by putting the two shell modes on the two toroidal cycles. fileciteturn35file10L416-L426 But I think **mean + gap** is cleaner than saying one toroidal radius is \\(H_0\\) and the other is \\(H_0+c\\). It isolates the common mode and differential mode first. Then we decide which geometrical coordinates represent them.\n\nAnd yes: your “Klein bottle is a Möbius torus” intuition is basically right, with one mathematical correction.\n\nA Klein bottle is not literally a torus made from a Möbius strip, but it can be constructed as the **mapping torus of a reflection of a circle**.\n\nFor the torus:\n\n\\[\n(\\phi+2\\pi,\\theta)\\sim(\\phi,\\theta).\n\\]\n\nGo around one cycle and the transverse orientation comes back unchanged.\n\nFor the Klein bottle:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(\\phi+2\\pi,\\theta)\\sim(\\phi,-\\theta).\n}\n\\]\n\nGo around one cycle and the other coordinate gets reflected.\n\nThat is exactly the “Möbius torus” intuition.\n\nEven better:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{T^2\\text{ is the orientable double cover of }K^2.}\n\\]\n\nAnd that fact may be extremely useful here.\n\nBecause suppose our two local shell states are represented by\n\n\\[\n+a,\\qquad -a.\n\\]\n\nIn the ordinary torus/double-cover description they remain distinguishable:\n\n\\[\n+a\\rightarrow+a,\n\\qquad\n-a\\rightarrow-a.\n\\]\n\nBut in the Klein quotient, one trip around the relevant global cycle gives\n\n\\[\n+a\\rightarrow-a.\n\\]\n\nThe identities exchange.\n\nThen locally there really are two shells:\n\n\\[\nR-a,\\quad R+a.\n\\]\n\nGlobally there may be only **one twisted radial degree of freedom**.\n\nThat gives an unexpectedly precise interpretation of:\n\n> shell/shell versus one Klein-type object.\n\nIt could literally be:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{two-shell description}\n=\n\\text{orientable double-cover description}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Klein description}\n=\n\\text{globally identified one-object description}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is considerably more satisfying than simply declaring “we used to have spheres, now we have a Klein bottle.”\n\nAnd it also preserves “both.”\n\nThe torus and Klein descriptions need not compete. The torus can be the **unwrapped cover** in which orientation and the two local sheets are easy to track. The Klein-type quotient can be the global identification.\n\nNow lift that out of the 2D cartoon.\n\nI don't think the literal claim should be “the 4D universe is a Klein bottle,” because \\(K^2\\) is two-dimensional.\n\nThe proper generalization is a **mapping torus**.\n\nTake whatever spatial/resolving fiber \\(\\Sigma\\) the model ultimately requires and some map\n\n\\[\nf:\\Sigma\\rightarrow\\Sigma.\n\\]\n\nConstruct\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM_f=\n\\frac{\\Sigma\\times[0,1]}\n{(x,1)\\sim(f(x),0)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf\n\n\\[\nf=\\mathrm{id},\n\\]\n\nwe have the untwisted/orientable cyclic version.\n\nIf \\(f\\) contains an orientation reversal,\n\n\\[\n\\det Df<0,\n\\]\n\nwe have the higher-dimensional analogue of the Klein construction.\n\nThen put the **worldtube fabric inside that**:\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal W=\\bigcup_i W_i\\subset M_f.\n\\]\n\nNow “the worldtubes go through the donut, around it, inside it, and perhaps all three” becomes mathematically ordinary.\n\nDifferent tubes occupy different winding/homotopy classes.\n\nIn the toroidal cover you might characterize a simplified tube by winding numbers\n\n\\[\n(p,q,n,\\ldots),\n\\]\n\nwhere one index counts major-cycle winding, another minor-cycle winding, another internal superhelical winding, etc.\n\nSo:\n\n- “around” = major-cycle winding;\n- “through” = minor/meridional winding;\n- “within” = internal framed twist of the tube;\n- “all three” = a worldtube carrying all those winding numbers simultaneously.\n\nThat is not decorative topology anymore. It supplies places for the several kinds of information we've been distinguishing:\n\n\\[\n\\text{spin},\n\\quad\n\\text{twist},\n\\quad\n\\text{writhe},\n\\quad\n\\text{link},\n\\quad\n\\text{global winding},\n\\quad\n\\text{higher correlations}.\n\\]\n\nThe archive already has the worldtube/filament picture as the structural primitive and the dual-shell differential as its clock structure. fileciteturn37file6L102-L104\n\nSo I think the minimal geometry becomes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{mapping-torus background}\n+\n\\text{finite-core framed worldtube fabric}\n+\n(R,\\Delta)\n}\n\\]\n\nwith \\(\\Delta\\) the clock/light gap.\n\nThat is much less machinery than “two hyperspherical universes plus torus plus Klein bottle plus timesheet.”\n\nThey become charts.\n\nNow: how does this map into Minkowski?\n\nLocally, throw away the global topology.\n\nA tiny observer doesn't see the donut or Klein identification. They see a tangent neighborhood.\n\nLet \\(u\\) be the local radial/clock direction and decompose a displacement:\n\n\\[\ndX=dX_\\perp+u\\,d\\sigma.\n\\]\n\nThe desired local readout is:\n\n\\[\nds_{\\rm obs}^2\n=\ndX_\\perp^2-d\\sigma^2.\n\\]\n\nPutting\n\n\\[\nd\\sigma=c\\,d\\tau\n\\]\n\ngives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nds^2\n=\ndx^2+dy^2+dz^2-c^2d\\tau^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nMinkowski.\n\nThe old metric-induction shorthand\n\n\\[\ng_{\\rm eff}\n=\n\\delta-2u\\otimes u\n\\]\n\ndoes exactly that algebraically: the radial direction gets the opposite sign while the transverse three remain positive.\n\nBut there's an important rigor correction already preserved in the archive: a positive Euclidean ensemble tensor does **not** magically become Lorentzian by inversion; the Lorentzian light cone has to emerge from the clock map plus the quadratic effective action/principal symbol. The current control stack explicitly says:\n\n\\[\n\\text{worldtube ensemble}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{resolving hypersurface}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{effective action}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{principal symbol}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{light cone}.\n\\]\n\nfileciteturn37file8L141-L169\n\nSo:\n\n\\[\ng_{\\rm eff}=\\delta-2u\\otimes u\n\\]\n\nis a very good **candidate coordinate/readout map**.\n\nIt is not yet the derivation.\n\nThat distinction should stay.\n\nThe \\(w\\)-map point could make this even simpler. I couldn't recover the exact “we may be seeing our own light cone” passage from these two compilations, so I don't want to pretend I did. But if the intended \\(w\\)-map is the radial fourth-coordinate/readout we've discussed, then geometrically the implication is straightforward:\n\nWhat looks like a cosmological shell need not be a physical material shell.\n\nIt can be:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{our past/null cone intersecting the larger worldtube geometry}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen the “shell” is partly observational geometry.\n\nThat would make the progression:\n\n\\[\n\\text{physical global manifold}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{worldtube fabric}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{null resolving cone}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{apparent spherical universe}.\n\\]\n\nAnd yes—then we might very literally be mapping the geometry of **our own light cone** rather than looking outward at an independently privileged spherical surface.\n\nThat would strongly favor keeping \\(R_s,R_\\tau\\) as **readout level sets**, not fundamental material shells.\n\nNow the standard-physics mapping becomes surprisingly orderly.\n\nFor Minkowski:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{local flat tangent/readout limit of }M_f.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe global torus/Klein topology disappears locally.\n\nFor GR:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{coarse-grained geometry of the worldtube ensemble}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe average configuration determines an effective\n\n\\[\ng_{\\mu\\nu},\n\\quad\n\\Gamma^\\rho_{\\mu\\nu},\n\\quad\nR^\\rho{}_{\\sigma\\mu\\nu}.\n\\]\n\nLocally, worldtube trajectories have to reduce to geodesics of this metric.\n\nCosmologically:\n\n\\[\nR(t)\\leftrightarrow a_{\\rm FLRW}(t)\n\\]\n\nat the appropriate coarse-grained level,\n\nwhile \\(c\\) fixes the local null cone.\n\nThe global Klein/mapping-torus identification would be extra **global topology**, not a modification of the local Einstein equations.\n\nThat's important.\n\nGR is perfectly capable of living on manifolds with nontrivial topology. fileciteturn37file14L355-L364\n\nSo the clean hierarchy might be:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM_f,\\mathcal W\n}\n\\]\n\nfundamental SAT/H(s)H representation\n\n\\[\n\\downarrow\n\\]\n\nlocal Here we draw parallels to three areas: category theory, homotopy type theory, and modal provability logic.\n[L23] \t•\tCategory Theory (Fixed-Point Theorems): In category theory, results like Lawvere’s fixed-point theoremformalize the essence of diagonal arguments (self-reference) in a very general setting. It shows that any sufficiently powerful category (a Cartesian closed category with a “well-behaved” self-mapping) will have a fixed point – an analog of a self-referential sentence. In simple terms, it implies that any theory expressive enough to talk about its own statements cannot be fully complete, because one can construct an object (or statement) that maps to itself under a certain diagonalizing morphism en.wikipedia.org\n[L26] . This is essentially Gödel’s argument in categorical language. Thus, category theory inherently contains a notion analogous to Gödel sentences. You could think of ж in categorical terms as an endofunctor on the category of theories or proofs that adjoins a new fixed-point object to avoid a paradox. Category theory doesn’t call it “ж”, but the idea of adding the missing fixed point appears in constructs like reflective subcategories or elementary topoi with truth objects. However, the incompleteness remains: Lawvere’s result shows any such attempt yields a new fixed point in the extended system too. So in category-theoretic frameworks, we already see the pattern “construct fixed-point → get new unresolvable point” abstractly. There isn’t a standard notion of a “rotational eversion” operator in category theory beyond this; rather, category theory confirms that any formal system strong enough for self-reference will need an infinite (or external) context to capture all truths – aligning with the role of ж.\n[L27] \t•\tHomotopy Type Theory (HoTT): Homotopy type theory is a modern foundation for mathematics that interprets logical propositions as types and proofs as geometrical constructions (homotopies). Could HoTT avoid incompleteness or have an operator like ж? In practice, HoTT still obeys Gödel’s incompleteness. It is a formal system (with an enumerable syntax and rules), so Gödel’s theorem applies – there are true statements about natural numbers it cannot prove \n[L28] cstheory.stackexchange.com\n[L29] . The authors of the HoTT book were well aware that HoTT is incomplete cstheory.stackexchange.com\n[L30] . So HoTT does not magically circumvent incompleteness; it “suffers” from it just as ZF set theory or Peano arithmetic do cstheory.stackexchange.com\n[L31] . However, HoTT introduces new principles (like the Univalence Axiom and higher inductive types) that were independent of previous foundations. In a sense, adding Univalence to homotopy type theory was akin to applying a ж-like step: a new axiom that wasn’t provable from the rest, expanding the system’s strength. As part of this endeavor, Hilbert introduced the epsilon calculus, an extension of formal languages by the epsilon operator. This operator substitutes for quantifiers and was intended as a method to prove consistency within extended formal languages.  Wikipedia+1Wikipedia+1Wikipedia\n[L370] Diagonal Lemma:\n[L371] The diagonal lemma establishes the existence of self-referential sentences in formal theories of natural numbers. These self-referential sentences are crucial in proving fundamental results like Gödel's incompleteness theorems and Tarski's undefinability theorem. The lemma demonstrates how certain statements can assert their own unprovability, leading to inherent limitations within formal systems.  Wikipedia+1Wikipedia+1\n[L372] Implications:\n[L373] While introducing self-referential axioms or operators can enrich a formal system, they do not entirely eliminate the challenges posed by Gödel's incompleteness theorems. These theorems reveal intrinsic constraints in formal systems capable of expressing basic arithmetic, indicating that no such system can be both complete and consistent. However, by carefully designing systems with specific limitations or extensions, it's possible to navigate some of these constraints, leading to self-verifying or self-referential frameworks.\n[L374] In essence, the exploration of self-referential axioms and systems offers valuable insights into the foundations of mathematics and logic, highlighting both the potential and the inherent limitations of formal systems.\n[L375] Sources\n[L376] ￼\n[L377]\n[L378]\n[L379] Nathan McKnight said:\n[L380] I like the idea of a self-proving operator... but, isn't = or ≡ already that?\n[L381]\n[L382] ChatGPT said:\n[L383] Yes, in a sense, equality (=) and equivalence (≡) already behave as self-proving operators—but they do so in a limited way because they operate within a given formal system rather than as a tool for self-eversion of the system itself.\n[L384] 1. What Does \"Self-Proving\" Actually Mean?\n[L385] When we talk about a self-proving operator, we mean something that:\n[L386] \t•\tDoes not require external validation—it is intrinsically true by its own structure.\n[L387] \t•\tBridges the gap between proof and truth—so that a formal system can verify its own axioms dynamically.\n[L388] \t•\tEverts the Gödelian boundary—so that what was previously \"unprovable\" is naturally included in a higher-order reasoning structure.\n[L389]\n[L390] 2.
