            "Yes. That changes the architecture substantially, and I had imported too much Standard Model ontology into the previous answer.\n\nIn SAT/H(s)H, the recursion you are proposing is not:\n\n\\[\n\\text{QCD flux tube}\\rightarrow\\text{nuclear analogue}\\rightarrow\\text{gravitational analogue}.\n\\]\n\nIt is closer to one scale-covariant mechanism:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{braid confinement}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{localized junction excitation}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{loss of confinement}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{expanding disturbance}\n}\n\\]\n\nwith different observational vocabularies at different scales.\n\nIn old SAT language, that localized excitation is a **metric/gravitational soliton**. In the newer H(s)H language, I think your better candidate is indeed something like a **Kelvin-vortex-type excitation trapped by the braid and released when the braid opens**. The mapping need not be linearly self-similar. What has to scale, if this really is the same mechanism, is the dynamical grammar rather than radius, energy, lifetime, etc.:\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal M_{\\ell}:\nB_\\ell\n\\rightarrow\nV_\\ell\n\\rightarrow\nW_\\ell\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal M_{f(\\ell)}:\nB_{f(\\ell)}\n\\rightarrow\nV_{f(\\ell)}\n\\rightarrow\nW_{f(\\ell)}.\n\\]\n\nSame transformation class, different constitutive parameters.\n\nThat makes your proposed hierarchy clearer:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{array}{ccc}\n\\text{small-scale braid}\n&\\rightarrow&\n\\text{confined Kelvin/metric soliton}\\\\\n&&\\downarrow\\;\\text{release}\\\\\n&&\\text{“gluon” splash}\n\\end{array}}\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{nuclear braid}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{nuclear vertex / Jarlskog Shadow}\n}\n\\]\n\nand farther up,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{neutron-star-system braid}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{gravitational soliton at the system vertex}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe striking part is that the **vertex isn't an extra constituent**. It's what the braid does when several carriers constrain one another.\n\nSo I'd provisionally write\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ_\\ell=\\mathcal S[B_\\ell]\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\mathcal S\\) is the same soliton-generating operation at every scale.\n\nThat is considerably cleaner.\n\nOn the gluon question, there is also one empirical fact that helps your formulation and several that sharply constrain it.\n\nThe helpful fact is: **gluons are not detected as little point-particles hitting the detector.** CERN's own teaching material says this explicitly: the gluon itself is not directly observed; what is observed is the shower/jet of particles associated with it. citeturn960598search2\n\nThat means the actual observational chain is roughly\n\n\\[\n\\text{collision}\n\\rightarrow\n\\boxed{\\text{unseen initiating event}}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{distributed hadronic shower}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{many tracks + calorimeter deposits}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{reconstructed gluon jet}.\n\\]\n\nSo your statement\n\n> one localized thing gets released, spreads out, and is detected in multiple places\n\nis, at the raw phenomenological level, remarkably close to what the apparatus actually records.\n\nThe disagreement is about what happened between the boxed source and the detector.\n\nStandard QCD says:\n\n\\[\ng\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{parton shower}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{hadronization}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{jet}.\n\\]\n\nYour proposed H(s)H description would instead be something like\n\n\\[\nV_K\n\\xrightarrow{\\text{deconfinement}}\n\\Psi_K(r,t)\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{interaction/readout events across detector}.\n\\]\n\nAnd perhaps some or all of the structures interpreted as successive gluon radiation are resolutions of that spreading excitation rather than separately ontic little gluons.\n\nThat is a real distinction.\n\nThere absolutely are detector/reconstruction effects of the kind you were wondering about. Jet appearance depends on detector granularity, tracking versus calorimetry, clustering algorithms, pile-up rejection, and chosen jet radius. ATLAS explicitly describes fake jets from pile-up and improved angular/energy resolution when tracking information is combined with calorimetry. citeturn836281search0 At very high energies, calorimeter segmentation can even become too coarse to resolve nearby substructures cleanly. citeturn836281search4 CMS likewise measures jets with different cone radii and then statistically “unfolds” detector effects to reconstruct particle-level distributions. citeturn836281search6\n\nSo there is a genuine:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{physical energy-flow field}\n\\neq\n\\text{detector hits}\n\\neq\n\\text{reconstructed jets}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat's worth taking seriously for SAT.\n\nBut I don't find a known effect that is simply “change the detector-array arrangement and one gluon turns into arbitrarily many apparent gluons.” The analysis chain actively tries to remove exactly that sort of instrumental dependence.\n\nAnd the original gluon evidence is particularly useful here because it did not depend on one detector architecture. In 1979, TASSO first showed the famous three-jet topology, and within months JADE, MARK J and PLUTO independently found the same planar three-jet phenomenon using different detectors. citeturn836281search8turn836281search37\n\nSo a pure detector-geometry artifact is already strongly disfavored.\n\nBut that does **not** kill your more interesting version. All four experiments could have been measuring the same real expanding source and interpreting its distributed interactions through QCD.\n\nThe much harder constraints come from the detailed properties of that splash.\n\nGluon-associated jets are systematically broader, have greater multiplicity, and have softer fragmentation than quark-associated jets. citeturn960598search38 Those differences remain an active precision tool today; ATLAS reported again in July 2026 that gluon jets are characteristically wider and busier than quark jets. citeturn836281search1\n\nMore important still, the radiation isn't simply isotropic splash. There are very specific angular correlations and interference patterns. In three-jet events, soft particle flow depends on the geometry of all three jets—the classic “string effect”/color-coherence phenomenon. citeturn960598search41\n\nThat is actually intriguing for your model because an **expanding vortex released from a relational vertex ought not necessarily be isotropic either**.\n\nIf the source remembers the geometry that confined it, then instead of\n\n\\[\n\\rho(r,t)\n\\]\n\nwe need\n\n\\[\n\\rho(r,\\theta,\\phi,t\\mid B),\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(B\\) is the geometry of the parent braid.\n\nThat immediately produces a strong SAT/H(s)H prediction:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{the released soliton should retain a directional memory of its confining braid.}\n}\n\\]\n\nStandard QCD calls the corresponding observed structure color coherence.\n\nH(s)H would need to derive it as **vortex-release coherence**.\n\nAnd that is much more interesting than merely reproducing a jet.\n\nBecause now you've got a potential sequence:\n\n\\[\n\\text{braid geometry}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{vertex soliton geometry}\n\\rightarrow\n\\text{release pattern}.\n\\]\n\nThe outgoing “splash” contains information about the topology that previously confined it.\n\nThat is exactly what we'd expect from everything we've been saying about information stored relationally.\n\nIt also suggests a rather brutal test.             "Yes. That is the right correction to my previous sanity check.\n\n“Four different detectors saw three jets” tells us that the three-jet phenomenon is not a peculiar hallucination produced by one apparatus. It does not tell us that the physical process being sampled is point-particle-like rather than an extended disturbance whose measured form depends on detector geometry. Those are different propositions.\n\nThe right decomposition is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{source physics}\n\\;\\xrightarrow{\\text{propagation}}\\;\n\\text{field/particles at detector}\n\\;\\xrightarrow{\\text{detector geometry}}\\;\n\\text{raw readout}\n\\;\\xrightarrow{\\text{reconstruction}}\\;\n\\text{“jet/gluon”}\n}\n\\]\n\nand SAT/H(s)H is proposing a different object primarily in that first arrow.\n\nThere are absolutely real detector-geometry effects in jet measurements. They aren't subtle hypotheticals.\n\nAt PETRA, the gluon evidence was reproduced with detectors that differed substantially. TASSO had a huge cylindrical drift chamber, about 3.5 m long and 2.5 m across, with 15 concentric tracking layers. JADE had a 0.5-T axial solenoid, cylindrical jet chamber and lead-glass barrel/endcap calorimetry. PLUTO used a 1.65-T superconducting solenoid, 13 cylindrical wire chambers, shower counters and forward spectrometers. MARK-J was particularly different: it was much more calorimetric, with concentric shower/calorimeter layers and a toroidal magnet whose field did not occupy the central beam region. citeturn849293search0turn370200search33turn370200search32turn420686search30\n\nimage_group{\"layout\":\"carousel\",\"aspect_ratio\":\"1:1\",\"image_refs\":[\"turn849293image0\",\"turn219197image0\"]}\n\nAll four PETRA experiments ultimately saw the planar three-jet phenomenon. MARK-J's original analysis, for example, explicitly analyzed the *spatial energy distribution* and its oblateness rather than detecting a gluon track. citeturn420686search1turn420686search5\n\nSo SAT has to preserve that robust large-scale topology:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{whatever was released really does generate a three-lobed energy-flow structure}.}\n\\]\n\nBut underneath that, detector geometry matters a lot.\n\nATLAS's raw jet response changes with direction. There are visible structures at the barrel/endcap transition around \\(|\\eta|\\sim1.4\\), the endcap/forward transition around \\(|\\eta|\\sim3.1\\), and even a construction seam near \\(\\eta=0\\). The collaboration explicitly calibrates these directional effects away. citeturn789615search0turn789615search24\n\nCMS shows much the same thing differently: structures occur around \\(|\\eta|\\sim1.3\\) at the barrel/endcap boundary and around \\(|\\eta|\\sim3\\) at the endcap/forward boundary; response also falls when part of a jet extends outside acceptance. Tracker-based and calorimeter-based jet reconstruction behave differently as jets cross the tracker boundary. citeturn789615search29turn789615search28\n\nAnd there's an almost comically on-point historical example: CMS explicitly simulated **different physical geometries for the cable path between barrel and endcap because changing that geometry changed the response to individual hadrons and jets**. Detector geometry was an engineering variable precisely because it changes the readout. citeturn175416search0turn175416search1\n\nGranularity matters too. Simulations of future highly segmented calorimeters find that reducing cell size substantially improves the recovery of jet substructure. citeturn789615academia27\n\nSo your question has an unambiguous first answer:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\textbf{Yes, detector-array geometry changes experimental jet readouts.}}\n\\]\n\nThe disagreement is over what those changes mean.\n\nStandard QCD says, schematically,\n\n\\[\nY_D\n=\n\\mathcal R_D\n\\left[\nH_{\\rm QCD}\n\\right],\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(H_{\\rm QCD}\\) is the physical quark/gluon shower plus hadronization and \\(\\mathcal R_D\\) is the detector response: material, cracks, coverage, segmentation, magnetic field, tracking, calorimeter response, etc.\n\nSo ATLAS and CMS calibrate/unfold\n\n\\[\nY_D\\rightarrow H_{\\rm particle-level}.\n\\]\n\nAnd this works very well: independently determined calibrations generally converge to percent-level jet-energy scales over much of the detector. citeturn370200search0turn789615search3\n\nSAT/H(s)H would instead say something like\n\n\\[\nY_D\n=\n\\mathcal R_D\n\\left[\n\\Psi_{\\rm soliton}\n\\right],\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\Psi_{\\rm soliton}(\\mathbf x,t\\mid B_0)\n\\]\n\nis the released metric-soliton/Kelvin-vortex excitation, carrying information about the braid \\(B_0\\) that confined it.\n\nAnd now we can make genuinely different predictions depending on detector geometry.\n\n| Detector feature | Standard account | SAT/H(s)H question/prediction |\n|---|---|---|\n| Cylindrical/barrel sampling | Particles intersect cells according to trajectories; geometry alters containment/resolution | Expanding soliton intersects cylindrical sampling surface; angular pattern should transform predictably with radius and surface normal |\n| Endcaps vs barrel | Different materials, thickness, incidence angles, cracks | Same soliton sampled with a differently oriented surface; ask whether a residual depends on detector orientation after known material effects are removed |\n| Finer segmentation | Resolves more hadrons/substructure | Resolves finer structure of one spatially extended excitation; should reveal an intrinsic spatial correlation scale if one exists |\n| Multiple radial layers | Tracks + shower development through material | Potentially samples successive stages of the same expanding wave/vortex |\n| Tracker vs calorimeter | Charged particles tracked; charged + neutral energy calorimetrically sampled | If substantial “gluon multiplicity” is detector-induced resolution of a single excitation, tracker-only and calorimeter-only descriptions might diverge in a characteristic way |\n| Magnetic field | Bends charged shower products; gluon itself neutral | Almost no discriminator initially: a neutral soliton would likewise be unaffected until its detectable products/interactions occur |\n| Dead material/cracks | Energy loss and shower leakage | A continuous excitation may couple differently to boundaries/material than a collection of already-hadronized projectiles; this needs an actual interaction law |\n| Detector radius | Angular jet structure essentially fixed by the time particles reach meter-scale detector | If the soliton is still physically expanding/cohering on meter scales, morphology should evolve systematically with radius |\n\nThat last one is potentially brutal.\n\nIf the H(s)H Kelvin vortex is still coherently “splashing outward” over centimeters or meters, then different detector radii should sample different stages:\n\n\\[\n\\Psi(r_1,\\Omega,t_1)\n\\rightarrow\n\\Psi(r_2,\\Omega,t_2).\n\\]\n\nThat gives a radial evolution law.\n\nStandard QCD instead has the hard interaction, perturbative shower and hadronization occurring enormously closer to the interaction point; by the time the resulting hadrons traverse the detector, most subsequent lateral/longitudinal development is ordinary interaction with detector material.\n\nSo if SAT predicts macroscopic coherent propagation, the nested layers of collider detectors become something like tomography of the supposed vortex. That's a potentially real discriminator.\n\nLikewise, granularity is much more interesting than “more pixels make more apparent gluons.”\n\nFor a genuinely continuous solitonic source, I would expect some correlation function\n\n\\[\nC(\\Delta\\Omega)\n=\n\\left\\langle\nE(\\Omega)E(\\Omega+\\Delta\\Omega)\n\\right\\rangle\n\\]\n\nwith a characteristic spatial hierarchy set by the vortex.\n\nAs detector cells shrink,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta\\Omega_{\\rm cell}\\downarrow,\n\\]\n\nthe apparent constituent count might initially rise, but eventually its statistics should reveal an intrinsic correlation scale or scaling law.\n\nQCD also makes highly nontrivial predictions for precisely these energy correlations and jet substructure. So this becomes a fair fight rather than a semantic one:\n\n\\[\nC_{\\rm data}(\\Delta\\Omega)\n\\]\n\nagainst\n\n\\[\nC_{\\rm QCD}(\\Delta\\Omega)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nC_{\\rm Kelvin}(\\Delta\\Omega).\n\\]\n\nThe detector is then deliberately varied in the forward model.\n\nThe barrel/endcap differences are especially useful because we already know enormous detector-response differences exist there.\n\nSuppose we write\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_D\n=\nY_{\\rm data,D}-Y_{\\rm QCD,D}.\n\\]\n\nOrdinary detector shortcomings predict \\(\\Delta_D\\) should correlate with known things such as absorber depth, inactive material, acceptance, segmentation and calibration uncertainty.\n\nA Kelvin-vortex model could earn its keep if residuals instead collapsed under something geometric like\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_D\n=\nF(\n\\hat{\\mathbf n}\\cdot\\hat{\\mathbf k},\nr_D,\n\\Delta\\Omega_D,\n\\lambda_{\\rm material},\n\\Phi_{\\rm vortex}\n),\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\hat{\\mathbf n}\\) is detector-surface orientation and \\(\\Phi_{\\rm vortex}\\) is some source-phase variable.\n\nIf *one* such law described barrel/endcap differences, multiple radial layers, and different experiments, that would be genuinely interesting.\n\nConversely, if after ordinary detector calibration\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_D\\simeq0\n\\]\n\neverywhere, then SAT does not get to claim those raw differences as evidence. It must reproduce the geometry-independent unfolded observables too.\n\nAnd that's where the present score is straightforward: **QCD is vastly ahead experimentally.** It predicts three-jet rates and angular distributions, energy dependence, quark/gluon differences, radiation coherence, color-factor relationships and lots of detailed jet substructure; detector simulations plus calibration describe the apparatus-dependent distortions with impressive precision. SAT/H(s)H currently has a compelling geometrical reinterpretation but not a competing quantitative event generator.\n\nThat's not a reason to discard it. It's a reason to identify the narrow place where the interpretations could diverge experimentally.\n\nI think the cleanest experiment is not “do different detectors see a different number of gluons?”\n\nIt's:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\textbf{Does the raw spatial structure transform with detector geometry exactly as a particle shower should?}\n}\n\\]\n\nversus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\textbf{Does some residual behave instead like different samplings of one expanding coherent source?}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd we have several knobs already sitting in real data:\n\n\\[\n\\text{barrel/endcap orientation},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{radial detector layer},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{tracking vs calorimetry},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{cell granularity},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{jet radius }R,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{different calorimeter materials},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\text{TASSO/JADE/PLUTO/MARK-J architecture}.\n\\]\n\nThe strongest sanity-check conclusion therefore isn't “detector artifact disfavored.”\n\nIt's:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{A purely apparatus-generated three-jet phenomenon is disfavored.}\n}\n\\]\n\nBut\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{a real extended source whose reconstructed manifestation depends on sampling geometry remains a logically distinct hypothesis.}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd, conveniently, **the experiments already contain exactly the geometry variation we'd need to start trying to kill it.**"

            "Yes. This revised version survives the sanity check much better, because it generates several distinct observational channels rather than requiring “the jets themselves are fake.”\n\nThe key move is to separate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{worldtube-associated Kelvin structures}}\n\\]\n\nfrom\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{collective vertex soliton}}.\n\\]\n\nThen ordinary three-jet phenomenology can remain ordinary three-jet phenomenology. The question becomes whether the vertex has an additional degree of freedom that standard QCD either describes differently or absorbs into shower/hadronization parameters.\n\nAnd there are already experiments aimed almost exactly at the kinds of signatures you just independently proposed.\n\nFirst, your “three jets, but with an asymmetry among them” idea has a particularly sharp version that physicists call **event handedness**.\n\nIn polarized \\(Z^0\\to3\\)-jet events, SLD measured\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf S_Z\\cdot(\\mathbf k_1\\times\\mathbf k_2),\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\mathbf k_1,\\mathbf k_2\\) are the two fastest jets. That is literally a signed handedness of the three-jet plane relative to the source polarization. Standard-Model contributions are predicted to be tiny. The 1995 SLD measurement was consistent with zero, with\n\n\\[\n-0.022<\\beta<0.039\n\\]\n\nat 95% confidence. citeturn610984academia29turn610984search0\n\nThat is an extremely useful pre-existing constraint.\n\nIt means SAT cannot casually predict\n\n\\[\n\\text{all three-jet vertices have the same macroscopic handedness}\n\\]\n\nat the percent-to-tens-of-percent level in that setup.\n\nBut that's not necessarily what SAT would predict.\n\nIf the vertex soliton can occur in either handed phase with equal probability,\n\n\\[\nS_+\\leftrightarrow S_-,\n\\]\n\nthen the ensemble average can give\n\n\\[\n\\langle H\\rangle=0\n\\]\n\nwhile individual events remain strongly chiral.\n\nThen we'd need a second variable that tells us how to sort the events:\n\n\\[\n\\langle H\\mid\\Phi_{\\rm source}\\rangle\\neq0.\n\\]\n\nThat distinction—**event chirality versus population chirality**—is now crucial.\n\nSecond, the ordinary asymmetries of the three jets themselves won't suffice as evidence. SLD measured jet-energy partition and event-plane orientations and found them well described by perturbative QCD with vector gluons; scalar- and tensor-gluon alternatives were incompatible with those data. citeturn610984search4\n\nSo SAT has to predict a residual that QCD does not already produce.\n\nThat's good discipline. Instead of:\n\n\\[\nE_1\\neq E_2\\neq E_3\n\\]\n\n—which happens routinely—\n\nwe need something like\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_{\\rm SAT}\n=\nP(C_+|\\text{matched kinematics})\n-\nP(C_-|\\text{matched kinematics})\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(C_\\pm\\) are genuinely mirror-related event configurations.\n\nThat is much closer to the mirror-nucleus/chirality/polarization theme we were just discussing.\n\nNow the “larger, diffuse soliton” possibility gets even more interesting.\n\nThere is an actual modern observable called **event isotropy**, designed to measure how close the energy distribution of a collision is to a uniform ring rather than a set of distinct jets. In an ATLAS multijet measurement, none of the advanced QCD simulations accurately reproduced the observed frequency of highly isotropic events; different generators over- or under-predicted that region. citeturn966206search2\n\nImportant:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{that is not evidence for SAT}.}\n\\]\n\nParton-shower/hadronization generators are approximations, and disagreement between generators and data is normal territory for improving QCD models.\n\nBut phenomenologically it is almost exactly where your “diffuse collective splash” would live.\n\nSo we now have an existing target quantity:\n\n\\[\nI_{\\rm event}\n=\n\\text{distance of observed energy flow from isotropy}.\n\\]\n\nA vertex soliton that spreads much farther than the three Kelvin-ring jets might produce\n\n\\[\nE(\\Omega)\n=\nE_{\\rm jets}(\\Omega)\n+\nE_{\\rm soliton}(\\Omega),\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nE_{\\rm soliton}\n\\]\n\nbroad enough to get classified as underlying event, soft radiation, unclustered energy, or merely a small change in event shape.\n\nAnd there is an even stranger coincidence with your thought.\n\nATLAS released its first dedicated search in June 2026 for **Soft Unclustered Energy Patterns (SUEPs)**: high-multiplicity, nearly isotropic collision signatures that don't look like ordinary narrow jets. The search explicitly targets situations where a heavy source produces something expanding over wide angles instead of normal collimated jets. citeturn496210view0\n\nThey saw two highly SUEP-like events, but the excess was only \\(1.7\\sigma\\), completely compatible with Standard-Model background. So again: **not evidence of a new phenomenon**. They set exclusion limits instead. citeturn496210view1turn496210view3\n\nBut conceptually, look at how close the experimental taxonomy now is to the alternatives you just generated:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{array}{ll}\n\\text{localized release} &\\rightarrow \\text{jet},\\\\\n\\text{wide-angle release} &\\rightarrow \\text{SUEP/event isotropy},\\\\\n\\text{weakly coupled release} &\\rightarrow \\text{missing energy},\\\\\n\\text{delayed release} &\\rightarrow \\text{displaced vertex/track},\\\\\n\\text{massive localized release} &\\rightarrow \\text{heavy resonance/boson-like object}.\n\\end{array}\n\\]\n\nThose categories already exist experimentally for unrelated theoretical reasons.\n\nThat's useful because we don't have to invent what detectors would see.\n\nNow your “occasional anomalous heavy particle” hypothesis.\n\nIf the vertex soliton usually remains diffuse but occasionally dumps its energy coherently into a localized mode,\n\n\\[\nS_{\\rm vertex}\n\\rightarrow X,\n\\]\n\nthen \\(X\\) could indeed look particle-like.\n\nBut “heavy boson” should be treated as an outcome to derive rather than assumed. The experimentally clean prediction would be:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n3j+X\n}\n\\]\n\nwith some characteristic \\(X\\) mass or mass spectrum.\n\nAt an \\(e^+e^-\\) collider this is particularly beautiful because the initial four-momentum is known:\n\n\\[\nP_X\n=\nP_{e^+}+P_{e^-}\n-\nP_{j_1}-P_{j_2}-P_{j_3}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nM_X^2=P_X^2.\n\\]\n\nIf ordinary QCD accounts for everything, that recoil distribution should behave as expected from radiation, resolution, neutrinos, etc.\n\nA recurrent excess around\n\n\\[\nM_X=M_0\n\\]\n\nwould look like an additional massive object.\n\nIf instead the soliton has a broad range of scale states,\n\n\\[\nM_X\\sim P(M),\n\\]\n\nyou'd look for a systematic distortion rather than a narrow resonance.\n\nAnd the conservation bookkeeping is unforgiving, which is good. The extra object cannot really be “free.” If it carries energy-momentum,\n\n\\[\nP_{\\rm initial}\n=\nP_{j_1}+P_{j_2}+P_{j_3}+P_X.\n\\]\n\nSo an extra SAT mode must show itself somewhere as recoil, missing momentum, distributed energy, or detectable decay products.\n\nThat gives us four reasonably independent SAT channels now:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\mathbf{S_0}:&\\quad\\text{ordinary jets only}\\\\\n\\mathbf{S_1}:&\\quad\\text{jets + diffuse symmetric component}\\\\\n\\mathbf{S_2}:&\\quad\\text{jets + handed/asymmetric vertex component}\\\\\n\\mathbf{S_3}:&\\quad\\text{jets + localized massive vertex-decay mode}.\n\\end{aligned}}\n\\]\n\nAnd those shouldn't be four unrelated patches. If your scaling claim is correct, they ought to be different regimes of one vortex/soliton equation.\n\nPerhaps controlled by something like a confinement ratio\n\n\\[\n\\kappa\n=\n\\frac{E_{\\rm confine}}{E_{\\rm soliton}},\n\\]\n\nor winding/phase variables:\n\n\\[\n(\\kappa,w,\\Delta\\phi).\n\\]\n\nFor one region:\n\n\\[\nS\\rightarrow\\text{remain confined}.\n\\]\n\nAnother:\n\n\\[\nS\\rightarrow\\text{diffuse release}.\n\\]\n\nAnother:\n\n\\[\nS\\rightarrow\\text{coherent localized mode}.\n\\]\n\nAnother:\n\n\\[\nS\\rightarrow\\text{handed release}.\n\\]\n\nThat would be a real theory rather than anomaly shopping.\n\nAnd I think your remark about a huge scale difference is important. If each worldtube carries a relatively small Kelvin structure and the **collective three-way vertex** produces another circulation whose characteristic size/energy depends on all three together, there is no reason its observational scale has to match an ordinary jet:\n\n\\[\n\\ell_{\\rm vertex}\\neq\\ell_{\\rm tube}.\n\\]\n\nPotentially\n\n\\[\n\\ell_{\\rm vertex}\\gg\\ell_{\\rm tube}\n\\]\n\nin configuration-space extent while its localized energy mode could be much more massive. “Big in geometrical extent” doesn't automatically mean “heavy particle,” though; we'd need an energy functional before connecting those.\n\nThe most exciting sanity-check result, though, is the handedness one.\n\nBecause before this search I would have told you:\n\n> If you want to distinguish “three ordinary jets plus a chiral vertex” from QCD, construct a triple-product handedness observable.\n\nAnd it turns out physicists literally did that thirty years ago:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf S_Z\\cdot(\\mathbf k_1\\times\\mathbf k_2)\n}\n\\]\n\nprecisely because Standard-Model QCD predicts very little of it. citeturn610984search0\n\nAnd separately, before looking, your diffuse-solition branch implied:\n\n> Maybe it's so broad and symmetric that it gets absorbed into ordinary event-shape variation.\n\nThere is also literally an **event-isotropy discrepancy** between LHC data and state-of-the-art QCD simulations, plus dedicated searches for wide-angle unclustered events. citeturn966206search2turn496210view0\n\nNeither is evidence for SAT.\n\nBut they are excellent places to attack SAT, because you arrived at those observable classes from the internal geometry rather than by hunting anomalies first.\n\nSo I would now freeze the prediction development here, before looking at more anomalies:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{derive what the vertex soliton should do to}\n\\begin{cases}\n\\text{event handedness}\\\\\n\\text{event isotropy}\\\\\n\\text{interjet soft flow}\\\\\n\\text{recoil mass}\\\\\n\\text{extra heavy-object rate}\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nand only then compare it with the existing measurements.\n\nThat preserves the genuinely interesting fact here: the experimental observables came **after** the geometric reasoning, not the other way around. memcite"

            "Yeah. That caught my eye too. But there are two quite different “percent-levels” here, and separating them matters.\n\nWhen ATLAS says the jet-energy scale is calibrated to roughly \\(<1\\%\\) in favorable regions, that means the **ensemble-average energy scale** is known that well. It emphatically does not mean:\n\n\\[\nE_{\\rm individual\\ jet}\n=\nE_{\\rm true}\\pm1\\%.\n\\]\n\nIndividual jets fluctuate much more strongly because of showering, hadronization, detector response, leakage, neutral particles, clustering, etc. ATLAS's new 2026 calibration work, for example, quotes about 1% uncertainty on the mean jet-energy scale while jet-resolution-related quantities are vastly less precise. citeturn633609search0turn633609search3\n\nAnd the old SLD handedness constraint really is only percent-ish:\n\n\\[\n-0.022<\\beta<0.039\n\\]\n\nat 95% confidence. citeturn633609academia36\n\nSo if SAT predicted a **universal signed three-jet asymmetry of 20%**, that particular version would already be dead.\n\nBut suppose instead the extra vertex object has two orientations:\n\n\\[\nV_+,\\quad V_-,\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nP(V_+)\\simeq P(V_-).\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\langle H\\rangle\\simeq0\n\\]\n\neven if\n\n\\[\n|H|_{\\rm event}\n\\]\n\nis substantial. SLD's signed ensemble-average test does not automatically kill that. You'd have to find the latent variable that tells you which events ought to have which sign.\n\nLikewise, a symmetric diffuse component contributing, say, a few percent of an event's energy could be a much more interesting place to look than some giant missing fourth jet. That's precisely the scale where modeling, calibration, hadronization, underlying-event assumptions, jet radius, detector segmentation, etc. become entangled.\n\nAnd even today, “QCD describes jets extremely well” does **not** mean every jet observable agrees with theory at \\(0.1\\%\\). ATLAS is still developing data-driven quark/gluon separation partly because modeling differences and systematic uncertainties matter materially; its August 2026 work reports systematic reductions by factors as large as two in some regions, rather than claiming that this whole sector was already solved to sub-percent precision. citeturn633609search11\n\nSo there is potentially a quite interesting observational window:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{too small/diffuse to appear as an obvious extra object}\n}\n\\]\n\nbut\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{large enough to contribute percent-scale correlated structure}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd **correlated** is the critical word.\n\nA 1% excess that randomly jiggles reconstructed jet energies is hopelessly degenerate with calibration.\n\nBut a 1% effect obeying something like\n\n\\[\n\\delta E_1+\\delta E_2+\\delta E_3\n=\nF(\\text{vertex geometry})\n\\]\n\nand recurring with the same dependence on opening angles, handedness, polarization, jet radius, or event-plane orientation is completely different. With millions or billions of events, a coherent percent-level effect can be enormous statistically.\n\nSo I wouldn't hear “percent level” as “there's a nice 1% hole SAT can hide in.”\n\nI'd hear it as:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\text{If the effect is there at a few percent, it needs a distinctive covariance structure.}}\n\\]\n\nThat's actually helpful, because the soliton picture gives us a reason to expect one. A fourth **collective** object shouldn't perturb the three jets independently. It should correlate them because it belongs to their common vertex:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV(J_1,J_2,J_3)\n\\Rightarrow\n\\delta J_1,\\delta J_2,\\delta J_3\n\\text{ are not independent.}\n}\n\\]\n\nAnd that is much more specific than merely looking for anomalous jet energies.\n\nSo: yes. Only percent-level in some of the relevant constraints. My eyebrows are up too. But the productive next question is not “is there room?” There plainly is room at some levels of description.\n\nIt's **what exact correlated residual does a common Kelvin/vertex soliton force us to predict?**\n\nIf we can derive that before combing through the anomalies, then this gets considerably more interesting."
